title: Characterisation of Scale Layer Structure and Resulting Mechanical Properties Under Varying Carbon and Chromium Contents
abstract: Abstract In hot forming processes and during heat treatment, scale layer formation occurs on the surface by temperatures over 570 °C. The structure of the scale layer depends on many different parameters, such as temperature, time, atmosphere and the alloying elements of the material. The aim of this work is to characterise the scale layer forming on steels with different carbon and chromium contents. Focus is on phase analysis using EDX and correlation of the iron oxide phases with hardness using nanoindentation. In addition to the well-known iron oxide phases and the three-layer-structure a fourth layer, called subscale, was identified, which primarily consists of chromium and silicon oxides. As this layer is the interface with the base material, it could influence the adhesion of the scale layer. The hardness measurements show high values in the area of the subscale, which indicates brittle fracture behaviour. The thickness of the subscale and the primary elements it contains depend on the alloying elements of the base material. For an unalloyed steel, the subscale thickness was reduced, compared to the low-alloy steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: For various process strategies in hot forming and heat treatment of steel materials, the heated surface reacts with the surrounding atmosphere at temperatures above 570 °C. In the presence of oxygen, oxide scales (metal oxides) are formed. For steel, three characteristic iron oxides occur: wustite FeO, magnetite Fe 3 O 4  and hematite Fe 2 O 3  [ 1 ]. Thereby, wustite is the innermost layer, magnetite the intermediate layer and hematite the outermost layer. The scale layer results in a significant material loss and also influences the hot forming process as well as the heat treatment due to the strong differences between the properties of the scale layer and the base material [ 2 ]. These properties are primarily dependent on the layer thickness and the individual layer structure. In [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ], it is shown that the scale layer formation depends on many process parameters, such as temperature, holding time, surface conditions as well as the furnace atmosphere. In studies on steels, it was found that the scale layer thickness is mainly influenced by the holding time and temperature of the oxidation, whereby the layer thickness increases with higher temperature and longer holding time in the furnace. The enhancement of diffusion processes with increasing temperature and process duration leads to the increase in scale layer thickness [ 7 ,  8 ]. In the case of steels with higher chromium contents (1–15 at. %), for example, the increased formation of chromium oxides with rising temperature hinders the diffusion processes [ 9 ]. The altered microstructure due to chromium precipitations and the combination of chromium spinels and chromium (III) oxide hinder the iron oxidation processes on the surface, which leads to reduced scale formation [ 10 ,  11 ]. For steels with additional aluminium content, it has been found, that below 800 °C, in particular chromium spinels slow down the oxidation processes. At higher temperatures, porous aluminium oxide layers form resulting in a significantly increased scale layer thickness [ 12 ]. Since a considerable number of different influencing factors and effects, such as passivation and microstructural changes in the base material, are noticeable with increasing alloying element contents, a brief overview of various alloying elements is given below: Noble elements such as nickel, cobalt and copper usually remain in the metallic phase and are not oxidised, but accumulate below the oxide layer [ 13 ]. Aluminium tends to lead to a reduction in scale adhesion, whereas silicon has a positive influence on the adhesion behaviour of the scale [ 14 ]. As manganese atoms replace the iron atoms in the lattice, the influence on scale formation and growth is assumed to be low [ 13 ]. Besides the alloying elements, the surface conditions affect the layer growth as well.

For pure iron in normal air under isothermal conditions (700–1,100 °C), the iron oxide distribution of hematite, magnetite and wustite is approximately 1:4:95. However,  Chen  et al. [ 1 ] found that the layer structure of steels can differ from that of pure iron. Ratios of magnetite to hematite of 1:4–1:5 were achieved, but also a ratio of 1:1 of wustite and magnetite. They attributed these differences to the additional alloying elements in the steel. In addition,  Malik  et al. [ 22 ] have identified a thin layer of graphite at the boundary between the scale layer and the substrate material.  Endo  et al .  [ 23 ] showed a thin Si-rich layer between the scale layer and the base material.  Wang  et al .  observed for a steel without additional chromium content for an oxide scaling temperature of 920 °C for 600 s no continuous spinel compound layer at the interface between the scale layer and the base material. In contrast, the chromium-containing steel formed a continuous Fe–Cr spinel intermediate layer during high-temperature oxidation [ 24 ]. This intermediate layer is in the literature referred as a porous subscale layer or, in short, a subscale. This is a porous zone directly beneath the outer scale layer at the interface between the metal and the oxide scale, which forms during the high-temperature oxidation of steel through internal oxidation, the diffusion of metal and oxygen ions as well as vacancy condensation [ 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. The subscale generally consists of microporosity, oxide particles or spinels, and alloying element oxides such as SiO₂ and Cr₂O₃ [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ].

In real applications, oxide scaling not only causes material loss but also increases tool wear and influences the shape of the workpiece due to the high hardness of the scale layer compared to the base material. However, not all iron oxides have the same hardness.  Huitron  et al .  [ 5 ] determined that wustite is the softest phase with the highest plasticity of all three iron oxides. Nanohardness tests by  Behrens  et al .  [ 25 ] also showed that wustite has the lowest hardness and hematite the highest hardness.  Graf  et al .  [ 26 ] determined a Vickers hardness of 1000 HV10 for hematite, 600 HV10 for magnetite and 400 HV10 for wustite.

Particularly in the field of hot forming, very complex stress states occur within the scale layer causing damage to the layer. Two main damage mechanisms have been identified known as cracking and delamination [ 27 ]. Cracking occurs, when the scale layer breaks due to stresses and/or excessive adhesive strength and brittle material behaviour of the scale layer [ 28 ]. At lower temperatures between 850 and 900 °C, cracks are initiated and grow along the scale layer to the interface connecting with other cracks [ 29 ]. During delamination, complete undamaged areas of the scale layer slide off the base material due to a lack of interface bond strength, when compared to the strength of the scale layer [ 30 ,  31 ]. This effect occurs at high temperatures between 900 and 1200 °C. The separation of the scale layer from the base material indicates a weak interface bonding between the base material and the scale layer [ 29 ].

In addition, the deformation behaviour of the scale layer also changes from elastic-brittle to plastic depending on the temperature. For compression tests on an scaled steel sample under rolling conditions, a reduction in the deformation of the scale layer was observed as the test temperature decreased [ 32 ].

In the work of  Wester  et al .  and  Behrens  et al .  [ 24 ,  25 ], the damage behaviour of scale layers formed on C45 and 45Cr4 with additional chromium content was investigated under real forging conditions. Flat tensile specimens were scaled in a dilatometer and then tested under tensile loading. The failure of the scale layer was recorded using an optical measuring system, and an evaluation algorithm based on computer vision approaches was developed and used to evaluate the acquired images. The scale layer exhibits different failure behaviour depending on the test temperature and strain rate. At low oxidation temperatures, ductile behaviour predominates, while higher oxide scaling temperatures lead to more brittle layer failure. In addition, a more ductile failure behaviour was observed for low strain rates. In contrast, the scale layer fails brittlely at higher strain rates. However, for the scale layer formed on the chromium-containing test alloy, only brittle layer failure was observed for all test conditions. Based on the above described research gaps, this thesis aims to investigate the influence of different chromium contents on the scale layer structure and the resulting mechanical properties as well as the subscale between the base material and the scale layer. In this case, the focus is on the hardness of the individual layer components and the damage behaviour under tensile stress.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs:
In this paper, the influence of different chromium contents in unalloyed and low alloyed steels on the scale layer structure and properties is investigated through separate and comparative analysis of the elements. Therefore, three steels were cast as round blocks using vacuum melting with falling casting and then forged into 40 mm round bars using open-die forging. The material was soft annealed after hot forming, creating a ferritic–pearlitic microstructure in all three steels before scaling. The aim was to ensure the best possible comparability. The chemical composition of the steels, determined by melt analysis, is listed in Table  1 .
 Table 1 Chemical composition of the three produced and tested steels. The chemical composition was determined by use of melting analysis Steel C Cr Si Mn P S Mo Ni Cu Al C45 0.49 0.1 0.2 0.42  < 0.004  < 0.001 0.034 0.081 0.096 0.021 45Cr3 0.49 0.6 0.2 0.42  < 0.004  < 0.001 0.034 0.081 0.096 0.021 45Cr4 0.49 1.15 0.2 0.42  < 0.004  < 0.001 0.035 0.076 0.100 0.017

The common and well-investigated unalloyed C45 steel is selected as a reference. Furthermore, two different Cr steels based on the C45, a 45Cr3 and a 45Cr4, were chosen (marked in Table  1 ). By using these steel alloys, the influence of three different chromium contents can be compared, while the influence of the carbon can be neglected due to the equal contents.

sections.heading: Scale Layer Formation and SEM Analysis
paragraphs: To analyse the scale layer structure forming on different steels in dependence of the alloying elements, the influence of temperature, time and atmosphere has to be equalised. Therefore, cylindrical samples with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 10 mm were oxidised at 1050 °C for 120 s for each steel. The tests were performed on a quenching dilatometer ( DIL805 A/D, Bähr, Germany ). Thereby, the samples were inductively heated with a rate of 15 K/s and a cooling rate of 10 K/s. The temperature was monitored and controlled using thermocouples type S (Pt/Pt–Rh). The closed test chamber of the dilatometer allowed inducing a protective atmosphere containing argon during heating and cooling to prevent pre- and post-scaling. During the oxide scaling process, the test chamber was flooded with normal atmosphere, so the oxidation occurred in flowing air. The heating and cooling rates, as well as the gas flow, were set identically over the entire trials. As a result of the selected process parameters, a well-adhesive scale layer with low number of pores could be produced. After the oxide scaling process, the samples were cold-embedded, sectioned and subsequently grounded from grid size 120 to 4000 and polished from 3 μm (Sat) to 1 μm (Dur) and finally oxide polished with 0.05 μm (MD-Chem) at automated grinding and polishing lines from Struers ( Struers, Copenhagen, Denmark ) and then vapour-deposited with carbon to create electrical conductivity. The SEM analysis (scanning electron microscope) was carried out using a LEO1455VP ( Zeiss AG, Oberkochen, Germany ) with ED(A)X (energy-dispersive analysis of X-rays) Genesis from  Zeiss . The samples were optically analysed using SE (secondary electrons) and BSD (backscattered electron) images to identify pores, cracks and the general layer structure as well as the layer bonding. The chemical composition of the scale layer was determined using three EDX spot measurements in each layer and quantified against an Fe 2 O 3  standard. As a final step, EDX mapping was performed where the elements Fe, O, Cr, Al, Mn and Si were recorded.

sections.heading: Nanoindentation
paragraphs: In addition to the chemical analysis of the scale layer, the hardness of the individual iron oxides was also be determined to characterise the separate layers. To achieve the highest possible resolution, the hardness was measured by nanoindentation using a Hysitron TI 950 TriboIndenter ( Bruker Corporation, Billerica, USA ). For the measurements, a highly precise three-axis tandem-tube piezoscanner was used with a capacitive three-plate transducer (2D transducer). The indentation was performed using a three-sided Berkovich diamond tip with a radius of less than 50 nm, directly attached to the transducer. The Berkovich tip was calibrated on a quartz glass specimen within a load range of 100 μN to 10,000 μN. The aim of these measurements was to generate hardness maps across the entire scale layer and additionally focused on the area of the subscale, at the interface between the scale layer and the base material. A normal force of 1800 μN was selected for the indentation tests and applied using a trapezoidal load function. The distance between the indentations was defined as 1.5 μm and applied within a measuring field of 120 μm × 120 μm for the examination of the entire layer structure. The indentations are perpendicular to the scale layer, using a cross section of the layer, in order to avoid the influence of indentation depth. For the subscale, the distance was reduced to 1 µm to increase the resolution in a measuring field of 18 µm × 198 µm. This approach enabled the individual identification of grains and pores within the scale layer without them influencing each other. The measuring fields were tactilely scanned using scanning probe microscopy (SPM) in order to rule out any overlap of the indents.

sections.heading: Crack Behaviour
paragraphs: To characterise the damage behaviour under uniaxial tensile loading of the scale layer, tensile tests were done based on the investigation by  Krzyzanowski  et al .  [ 29 ] and the experimental setup, procedure, and analysis of the tensile test were chosen analogous to those used by  Wester  et al .  [ 33 ], which updated the testing procedure of  Krzyzanowski . The tests were performed using a DIL 805 A/D + T forming simulator ( Bähr, Germany ).

For controlled oxidation, the flat tensile specimens were clamped in the dilatometer and inductively heated to the respective target temperature. Subsequently, the specimens were held at the target temperature for an oxidation time of 120 s and then tested at the same temperature. To analyse crack formation and the associated layer failure, the experimental setup was conducted as described in [ 33 ], using an optical 2D measurement system GOM ARAMIS ( Zeiss AG, Oberkochen, Germany ) on flat tensile specimens. Optical measurement allows for a spatially and temporally resolved analysis of the results. By using flat specimens, a larger surface area could be examined compared to the original setup by  Krzyzanowski  et al .  [ 29 ]. The experimental setup is schematically depicted alongside the specimen geometry in Fig.  1  A. The specimens (Fig.  1  B) were machined from forged semi-finished products using wire erosion. Fig. 1 A: Test setup in the dilatometer for oxide scaling and subsequent tensile testing of flat specimens with optical measuring system for identifying layer failure according to  Wester  et al .  [ 33 ]. B: Geometry and dimensions of the test sample

The detailed experimental plan is shown in Table  2 . The temperatures were monitored and controlled through welded-on thermocouples type S. Each parameter configuration was tested in three repetitions.
 Table 2 Testing parameters for the tensile test to determine the damage behaviour Oxide scaling and testing temperature in °C Heating rate in K/s Cooling rate in K/s Strain rate in 1/s 900, 950, 1000, 1050 and 1100 5 5 0.01

Own previous work from  Wester  et al .  [ 33 ] demonstrated a new evaluation method for the optical measurements based on computer vision. In this method, an area of interest on the specimen was first defined using a selection of different filters, and subsequently, formed cracks were automatically detected within this area. From the image captured at the time of initial crack formation, the technical strain of the specimen was determined based on the undeformed specimen shoulders. The critical strain obtained in this manner was considered a measure of the tolerable damage.

sections.heading: Influence of Chromium on the Chemical Composition of the Scale Layer via SEM
paragraphs: The primary goal was the chemical analysis of the scale layer to identify the influence of various chromium contents in the base material on the layer structure and the iron oxide distribution. Therefore, the previous scaled C45, 45Cr3 and 45Cr4 were prepared for SEM analyses. To identify suitable areas for EDX analysis within the scale layer, BSD and SE images of the scale layers were taken. Figure  2  shows images of the scale layer for the three materials C45 (A), 45Cr3 (B) and 45Cr4 (C). In BSD images, oxygen-rich phases appear darker compared to iron-rich phases. Assuming that hematite, magnetite and wustite occur, the classic layered structure can be identified from the BSD images. Hematite can be found on top of the scale layer, magnetite underneath, followed by wustite with a subscale between the scale layer and the base material. This structure is visible for each tested material. The iron oxide distribution of C45 and 45Cr3 is consistent, with a distribution of 1% hematite, 14% magnetite and 85% wustite. Only 45Cr4 shows a slightly different iron oxide distribution with 1% hematite, 39% magnetite and 60% wustite. Also noticeable is the separation of the scale layer from the base material for the 45Cr4. This was not observed for the other two steels. Fig. 2 BSD and SE images of the scale layer formed on C45 ( A ), 45Cr3 ( B ) and 45Cr4 ( C ) at 1050 °C for 120 s. The four layers forming the complete scale layer are visible: hematite, magnetite, wustite and subscale

To further characterise the scale layer, the layer thicknesses of the individual iron oxides were measured. For C45, the layer thicknesses for wustite are 55.66 ± 0.94 μm, for magnetite 14.43 ± 1.4 μm and for hematite 1.29 ± 0.35 μm for hematite. The 45Cr3 has a very similar layer thickness for wustite with 59.77 ± 2.02 μm, for magnetite with 11.77 ± 0.56 μm and for hematite with 1.08 ± 0.07 μm for hematite. Only the 45Cr4 shows a bigger change in iron oxide distribution for wustite with 37.83 ± 3.21 μm, for magnetite with 34.14 ± 2.37 μm and for hematite with 1.76 ± 0.44 μm for hematite. In addition to the three characteristic iron oxide layers, a subscale could be identified. This layer lies directly underneath the wustite layer attached to the base material and thus defines the connection of the entire scale layer to the base material. Figure  4  B shows a zoomed-in section of the subscale for 45Cr3. For every base material, the subscale could be observed, but the resulting thickness varied between 2.5 ± 0.26 μm for C45, 3.5 ± 0.48 μm for 45Cr3 and 4.7 ± 0.53 μm for 45Cr4. The layer thickness of each subscale and the three iron oxide phases were measured at 5 different locations over the cross section. The EDX analysis of the subscale revealed a mixture of various alloying elements in addition to iron and oxygen (see Table  4 ). Considerable contents of chromium (Cr) and silicon (Si) are found. Smaller amounts of the elements molybdenum (Mo), aluminium (Al) and manganese (Mn) were detected but are negligible. According to the literature [ 35 ,  36 ,  37 – 38 ], iron oxides, chromium oxides and silicon oxides can be expected in the subscale.

Fe and O show a relatively equal distribution across the three steels with an average value of approx. 28.0–33.8 at. % for Fe and approx. 52.3–57.6 at. % for O over three measuring points. There are significantly greater differences for Cr and Si. The unalloyed steel C45 showed a Cr content of 1.3 at. %, while the 45Cr3 and 45Cr4 have a significantly increased value of 6.3 and 6.0 at. %. For Si, the C45 shows significantly higher values with 11.1 at. % than the 45Cr3 with 8.1 at. % and the 45Cr4 with 3.9 at. %.

In addition to the EDX spots, EDX mappings were also performed on the steels C45 (A), 45Cr3 (B) and 45Cr4 (C) shown in Fig.  5 . The initial backscattered electron (BSD) images show the measured areas and the qualitative distribution of chromium (purple) and silicon (blue) in the scale layer and the base material. Clearly visible is the variation in the intensity, whereby higher intensities correspond to higher concentrations of the respective alloying elements relative to the surrounding areas. For Cr, a moderate concentration is observed in the base material for all three steels, with the concentration increasing proportionally to the Cr amount in the steel. Within the subscale, an elevated Cr concentration compared to the base material can be noticed while increasing significantly with higher Cr content in the base material. In contrast, Si does not follow this trend; its concentration remains comparable across all three materials. There are also no significant concentration differences between the subscale of the three steels. The only similarity with Cr is the increased Si concentration within the subscale compared to the base material. Other detected elements such as manganese, aluminium or copper are present at levels too low to be reliably distinguishable from background noise. An additional finding is the absence of all alloying elements in the iron oxide layers hematite, magnetite and wustite, where only Fe and O were detected. Fig. 5 The BSD images show the scale layers formed on C45 ( A ), 45Cr3 ( B ) and 45Cr4 ( C ) and indicate the measurement positions for the EDX mapping. EDX mappings of the elements chromium (Cr, pink) and silicon (Si, blue) are shown beneath. As the Cr content in the base material increases, the layer thickness and Cr content in the subscale also increase. No differences in the Si content of the different subscales could be detected

sections.heading: Hardness Mapping on Scale Layer
paragraphs:
The scale layers were tested over a large area by nanoindentation in order to visualise the mechanical properties of each iron oxide phase and the subscale as a mapping. Table  5  shows the mean values for wustite, magnetite, hematite, subscale and base material in GPa with standard deviation. Figure  6  presents the nanohardness mappings for C45, 45Cr3 and 45Cr4. All three mappings were examined and analysed for cross sections of the respective steel samples, from the substrate through the scale layers to the embedding medium. The substrate of the C45 sample (A) exhibits an average nanohardness of approximately 3.8 GPa, while the 45Cr3 (B) shows an average nanohardness of around 4.1 GPa. The 45Cr4 (C) demonstrates a significantly higher average nanohardness of approximately 7.3 GPa. Directly on the substrate, the subscale can be identified across all three materials, characterised by an average nanohardness of approximately 9.4–10 GPa. The nanohardness mapping within the scale layer reveals distinct regions corresponding to wustite and magnetite, which correlates well with the iron oxide distribution observed in SEM images and EDX analyses. Wustite shows an average hardness of around 5.5–5.8 GPa. Magnetite exhibits an average hardness in a range of 7.0–7.3 GPa for C45 and 45Cr3. For 45Cr4, it is lower with 6.0 GPa. These similar hardness values are also observed within regions of the scale layer, confirming the presence of magnetite precipitates within the wustite matrix through the hardness mapping. Furthermore, a hardness gradient towards the embedding medium was detected, which can be attributed to preparation effects, such as rounding of the edges during polishing. Notably, the edge areas within all materials exhibit very high hardness values of up to approximately 8.5 GPa. These hardness values are associated with hematite layer. However, this outer layer often cracked during preparation or nanoindentation, resulting in a limited number of reliable hardness values and no data for the Young’s modulus. In addition to hardness, the Young’s modulus was determined. The base material of all three steels shows a value between 200 and 208 GPa. The subscale exhibits lower values compared to the base material. For C45 146.5 GPa, for 45Cr3 142.8 GPa and for 45Cr4 133.9 GPa were measured. Wustite shows a value between 140 and 146 GPa and magnetite between 150 and 157 GPa. For hematite, the available data are insufficient to provide any information on its Young’s modulus. In order to obtain valid values at the edges of the scale layer, the indents were set at a sufficient distance from any global cracks.
 Table 5 The mean values of hardness and Young’s modulus in GPa are shown for wustite, magnetite, hematite, subscale and base material. There were not enough values for 45Cr4 and insufficient data on the standard deviation for C45 and 45Cr3 for the hematite Hematite Magnetite Wustite Subscale Base material C45 Hardness in GPa ≈ 8.5 7.3 ± 0.45 5.8 ± 0.45 9.9 ± 1.21 3.8 ± 0.39 Modulus in GPa – 156.7 ± 9.0 145.7 ± 8.6 146.5 ± 10.6 202.9 ± 12.0 45Cr3 Hardness in GPa ≈ 8.5 7.0 ± 0.47 5.6 ± 0.96 10.0 ± 1.08 4.1 ± 0.33 Modulus in GPa – 157.0 ± 7.5 142.9 ± 18.3 142.8 ± 12.9 207.2 ± 13.1 45Cr4 Hardness in GPa – 6.0 ± 1.5 5.5 ± 0.44 9.4 ± 1.18 7.3 ± 0.91 Modulus in GPa – 149.1 ± 7.9 140.8 ± 10.3 133.9 ± 11.8 200.5 ± 12.1 Fig. 6 Nanohardness mappings for the scale layer formed on C45 ( A ), 45Cr3 ( B ) and 45Cr4 ( C ) in GPa. Based on the nanohardness values, the following iron oxides could be identified: hematite, magnetite and wustite, as well as the magnetite phase within the wustite matrix and the subscale layer

As described in Sect. “ Hardness Mapping on Scale Layer ”, the subscale forms between the scale layer and the substrate material. This study aims not only on the general characterisation of the scale layer but also on the subscale, which has been insufficiently investigated thus far. Figure  7  displays a measurement field of the subscale which was scanned tactilely using scanning probe microscopy with a normal force of 2 µN. One field consists of 18 × 24 indents with a spacing of 1 µm. The hardness mapping in Fig.  7  B–D was each compiled from 8 measurement fields and present the hardness values in GPa for the subscale grown on the substrate materials C45, 45Cr3, and 45Cr4. For all three base materials, similar hardness values of approximately 9.4–10 GPa were observed in the subscale. As indicated via EDX measurements, the hardness mappings also reveal a weakly developed subscale for C45 and a progressively more pronounced subscale as the chromium content increases. Fig. 7 3D SPM image showing nanohardness mapping in the subscale of the C45 scale layer (A). The nanohardness mappings for the subscale formed on C45 (B), 45Cr3 (C) and 45Cr4 (D) in GPa are shown on the right. The subscale can clearly be detected through the high nanohardness values (13–14 GPa), which are higher than those of the surrounding phases with base material C45 and 45Cr3 (4.5 GPa), as well as wustite (5.5 GPa)

sections.heading: Crack Initiation Behaviour
paragraphs: Figure  8  shows the tensile tests for identifying scale layer failure, with the critical strain up to layer failure over the forming temperature for steels C45, 45Cr3 and 45Cr4. The samples were oxidised at the same temperature at which the tensile test was performed. For forming temperatures of 900 and 950 °C, there is a significant variation in the elongation where the layer failure was identified. The minimum tensile strain is approximately 0.006 and the maximum tensile strain is 0.047. Above 1050 °C, there is a significant reduced spread in the values between 0.01 and 0.015. Above 1050 °C, there are no differences between the three materials. The critical strain is approximately 0.0025. On average, a decrease in critical strain can be observed for all three starting materials as the temperature increases. Only the 45Cr3 for 900 °C represents an exception down to 0.01 in critical strain. Fig. 8 The critical strain over the deformation temperature of the scale layers formed on C45, 45Cr3 and 45Cr4 steels is examined. The oxide scaling temperature corresponds to the deformation temperature. Between 900 and 1000 °C, significant deviations occur in the elongation at which the layer fails. Above 1000 °C, the scale layers of the three steels are almost indistinguishable

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The SEM images in Fig.  2  show clearly the characteristic scale structure with a composition of 84% wustite, 14% magnetite and 1% hematite directly on the surface. The corresponding iron oxides could be identified either by the greyscale in the BSD images based on the oxygen content or by the EDX spots (see Fig.  3 ). The measured values shown in Table  3  demonstrate a high level of consistency for hematite with approximately 41 at. % Fe and 59 at. % O across all three investigated materials with less than 2.5% of deviation. For the magnetite phase, the measurements indicate a reasonable correlation to the work by  Young  et al .  [ 34 ] around 42.2 at. % Fe and 57.8 at. % O. The scale layer of 45Cr4 shows the expected chemical composition with 42.2 at. % Fe and 57.8 at. % O with 1.5% deviation. For C45 and 45Cr3, a bigger deviation up to 5.5% from the expected values is noticeable. This deviation can be explained by small measurement inaccuracies and the existence of pores inside the magnetite layer. The measurement spot with the selected process parameters has an approximately depth of 1.12–1.4 µm for FeO [ 39 ]. Even if the measurement has been taken on an apparently pore-free surface, pores may lie just below the surface and affect the measured values.

This thicker magnetite layer for 45Cr4 is caused by the separation of the scale layer from the base material. As soon as the scale layer starts to separate from the base material, a new scale layer forms on the exposed surface, binding the iron atoms and thereby significantly reducing the support for the overlying layer. This causes the iron-richest phase (FeO) to be consumed and leads primarily to the formation of magnetite and haematite [ 34 ,  40 ]. The identical effects could also be observed for C45 and 45Cr3, suggesting that chromium content is not a significant factor at this stage. However, detached scale layers are not suitable for the investigations in this paper, the focus has been placed on adherent layers and the separation of the scale layer cannot be discussed further. For wustite, the C45 with a chemical composition of approx. 49.3 at. % Fe and 50.7 at. % O demonstrates a high level of consistency with the literature data [ 34 ] and a maximum deviation of 1.5%. The measurements of the wustite layer from 45Cr3 and 45Cr4 reveal a slight deviation with 2.5% for 45Cr3 up to 5.6% for 45Cr4. Table  4  shows that the dark-appearing phases in the wustite matrix can be classified as magnetite based on their chemical composition. The proportion of Fe is 47.2 at. % and of O is 52.8 at. %. These deviations can be explained by the size of the measuring spot and the dark-appearing phases in the wustite. This finding is also consistent with the study by  Haapakangas  et al .  [ 41 ]. The dark-appearing phases are repeatedly measured in the wustite because the measuring spot also collects information below the surface. Therefore, the influence of the magnetite phases on the measured spots in the wustite cannot be excluded.

The subscale was identified as the fourth layer of the complete scale layer being the interface to the base material [ 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. It consists of Fe, O, Cr, Si [ 19 ,  20 – 21 ] and other alloying elements which are lower than 1 at. % (see Table  4 ). Only Cr and Si could be identified in higher quantities in the subscale for the three steels, due to the higher contents in the base material. The Fe and O proportions in the subscale are relatively consistent between the three steels. There are only small deviations, which do not follow any noticeable trend. A clear trend can be seen for Cr and Si. For the unalloyed C45, there is a very low proportion of Cr in the subscale. This fraction increases with increasing Cr content in the base material and reaches saturation at approximately 6.0–6.3 at. %. A reverse trend is noticeable for Si. As the chromium content in the base material increases, the proportion of Si in the subscale decreases. However, since the subscale is less prominent for C45 than for the other two steels, more Si is concentrated in the measured spot, relatively, and is distributed more evenly across the layer thickness in the other two scale layers. The Cr content in the subscale is increasing with increasing Cr content in the base material, which can also be seen in Fig.  5 . However, it is currently not possible to explain whether there is a maximum Cr content in the subscale, as the EDX spots show a small difference in the Cr content from 45Cr3 to 45Cr4 by 0.3% from 6.3 to 6.0. But both values are in the same range and show the maximum Cr content in the subscale for the tested materials. Furthermore, at this point, no predictions can be made about the exact phases in the subscale. Phase analysis using XRD might be a suitable option for investigating the subscale in the future.

The structure of the scale layer and the development of subscales depend not only on the chemical composition of the base material but also on temperature and time. This study only examined scale layers formed at 1050 °C for 120 min, and the following trends are only preliminary findings. The distribution of iron oxides: Wustite, magnetite and hematite, seems independent of the alloy system of the base material. However, the thickness and chemical composition of the subscale could depend directly on the alloying elements present in the base material. A higher content of alloying elements in the base material results in a thicker subscale. In addition to chemical analyses, the nanohardness tests enable mechanical characterisation of the scale layer and a preliminary classification of the properties of the subscale. The three hardness mappings of the scale layers from Fig.  6  A–C show that wustite is the softest layer, magnetite the second softest layer and hematite the hardest layer, which is in line with the studies by  Wester  et al .  [ 24 ] and  Behrens  et al .  [ 33 ]. For the magnetite phase, the hardness values of 45Cr4 (6.0 GPa) show a noticeable difference compared to those of C45 and 45Cr3 (7.0–7.3 GPa). This difference is clearly visible in the hardness mapping in Fig.  6  (C), where the upper part of the scale layer shows a decrease in hardness values towards the edge. This is associated with the strong cracking in this area of the scale layer. As the specified hardness value represents an average across the entire area of the magnetite layer, this value is lower compared to C45 and 45Cr3. But the maximum values remain between 7.0 and 7.5 GPa, which is comparable with the other two materials. In addition, these hardness mappings enable a classification and visualisation of the magnetite phases within the wustite matrix on the basis of each individual hardness and Young’s modulus value pair. Similarly to the EDX analyses, the different chromium contents in the base materials have no influence on the hardness distribution within the scale layer. An increase in hardness can be observed for the substrate material of 45Cr4 compared to C45 and 45Cr3. This can be explained by the higher chromium content in the base material which increases the cooling rate to form bainite and martensite under air cooling conditions. For C45 and 45Cr3, the microstructure consists of ferrite and perlite.

Nanohardness mappings of the subscale for all three steels (see Fig.  7  B–D) shows very high hardness values of 9.4–10 GPa for C45, 45Cr3 and 45Cr4. These values are reasonable given that silicon and chromium oxides are found in the subscale in addition to iron oxides. Lower hardness values of 2–4 GPa within the subscale indicate small to larger pores and show the high porosity of the subscale. For 45Cr4, areas with very low hardness are also visible below the subscale, indicating embedding material and showing that the scale layer is beginning to separate between the subscale and the substrate material. It can be concluded that the subscale acts as a weak point in the layer adhesion. Since the separation of the scale layer could only be observed in 45Cr4 with the thickest subscale, it can be assumed that above a certain thickness, higher amount of alloying elements or harder base material the separation of the layer becomes progressively easier.

The tensile tests on the scaled flat tensile specimens were an initial attempt to investigate the influence of the differently developed subscale for the three steels on layer failure and layer adhesion. The influence of different chromium contents in the base material on the thickness of the subscale is more pronounced at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures, as the growth of the subscale depends directly on the growth of the scale layer. Up to a forming temperature of 1000 °C, a decrease in critical strain was observed for C45, 45Cr3 and 45Cr4. Only for 900 °C of 45Cr3 was an outlier that cannot be explained yet. Above 1000 °C, the critical strains for all scale layers drop to a value of 0.0025. For oxide scaling and forming temperatures up to 1000 °C, the thinner and more compact layers provide greater resistance to tensile stress. Above 1000 °C, the scale layers begin to grow thicker, resulting in more pores forming within the scale layer, which contributes to earlier layer failure. In addition, the thicker subscale can further increase the instability of the entire layer. However, since no differences between the three base materials are apparent above 1000 °C, the influence of the subscale is considered negligible. Accordingly, no clear influence of the subscale on layer failure could be identified. The presented tensile method shows only layer failure in a unidirectional way and cannot provide any information’s about interfacial adhesion. The composition and structure of the subscale may be directly related to the adhesion of the scale. It is therefore necessary to adjust the test setup in further works in order to investigate layer adhesion.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The aim of the paper was to identify the influence of different chromium contents on the formation of the scale layer and layer failure. EDX analyses and nanohardness mappings provide an initial approximation of the mechanical properties of the subscale in correlation to the chemical composition. The results of this work are only representative for oxide scales formed at 1050 °C for 120 s and are subject to the mentioned measurement inaccuracies of the used measurement methods. The most important results are presented below: The well-known scale layer structure with wustite, magnetite and hematite could be verified using EDX analysis. Variations in the chromium content of the base material did not result in any changes to the resulting layer structure. The BSD and SE images revealed a fourth layer between the substrate and the wustite layer for each base material. This layer is defined as subscale and its thickness increases from 2.5 to 4.7 μm with increasing alloying element content (Cr) in the base material. In addition, the EDX mappings identified primarily the alloying elements Cr and Si in the subscale. Besides these alloying elements, Fe and O could be found within the subscale. It is hypothesised that the subscale consists of iron, chromium and silicon oxides but the phases were not identified in this work. This leads to the assumption that most of the alloying elements that are precipitated accumulate in the subscale not in the scale layer. Nanohardness mappings enabled the identification of all three typical iron oxides: hematite, magnetite and wustite, as well as the magnetite phases within the wustite matrix. The hardness distribution in the iron oxides corresponded to the well-known layer structure. The subscale showed extremely high hardness and high porosity, suggesting a solid but very brittle layer structure. Up to a temperature of 900–1000 °C, the critical strain decreases with increasing temperature. However, above 1000 °C, there is no change in the critical strain with increasing temperature. The tensile tests performed to identify the failure of the scale layer did not show any influence of the thickness variation of the subscale. For this purpose, future work will require a specific adhesion test for the scale layers, for example a shear pull-off test.

To sum up, existing knowledge about scale layer formation was confirmed, and new insights were obtained regarding the subscale as a function of different chromium contents. In order to describe the influence of different alloying elements on the subscale in more detail, further experiments using XRD and TEM analysis will be carried out to fully understand the influence of Cr on the structure and composition of the subscale and its failure behaviour. In order to make these findings usable for improved descaling in forming processes, new suitable test methods for investigating the layer adhesion need to be evaluated.
